WITH ql AS (SELECT quote_id, count(*) nl, sum(est_hours) hrs, sum(unit_price*quantity) price, sum(est_outside) outs, max(lead_weeks) lead FROM erp_quote_lines GROUP BY 1),
lh AS (SELECT ql2.quote_id, count(DISTINCT h.work_centre) nwc FROM erp_quote_lines ql2 JOIN erp_quote_line_hours h USING(quote_line_id) GROUP BY 1),
q AS (SELECT q.quote_id, estimator_id e, customer_id c, substr(sent_on,1,4) y, nl, ln(hrs+1) lh_, ln(price) lp, (outs>0)::int has_out, nwc FROM erp_quotes q JOIN ql USING(quote_id) LEFT JOIN lh USING(quote_id) WHERE kind='new' AND status IS NOT NULL AND status<>''),
cy AS (SELECT c,y,count(*) n,sum(nl) s1,sum(lh_) s2,sum(lp) s3,sum(has_out) s4,sum(nwc) s5 FROM q GROUP BY 1,2),
ce AS (SELECT c,y,e,count(*) n,sum(nl) s1,sum(lh_) s2,sum(lp) s3,sum(has_out) s4,sum(nwc) s5 FROM q GROUP BY 1,2,3),
d AS (SELECT q.e, nl-(cy.s1-ce.s1)/(cy.n-ce.n) d1, lh_-(cy.s2-ce.s2)/(cy.n-ce.n) d2, lp-(cy.s3-ce.s3)/(cy.n-ce.n) d3, has_out-(cy.s4-ce.s4)/(cy.n-ce.n) d4, nwc-(cy.s5-ce.s5)/(cy.n-ce.n) d5 FROM q JOIN cy USING(c,y) JOIN ce USING(c,y,e) WHERE cy.n>ce.n)
SELECT e, count(*) n, round(avg(d1),3) rel_lines, round(avg(d2),3) rel_log_hrs, round(avg(d3),3) rel_log_price, round(avg(d4),3) rel_outside_share, round(avg(d5),3) rel_work_centres FROM d GROUP BY e ORDER BY e

content.text:
**Verdict on F6: it stands with changes, and it is much weaker than written.** F6's numbers reproduce exactly (27.7 missing wins, $257,449, $33,837 a year, q312), but its explanation doesn't hold up. I saved the challenge as `challenge.json`.

**Why it changes:**
- **115 isn't an estimator.** HR lists them as an engineer (q276). Half of their new quotes (217 of 430) fall in 14 months right after estimators left: 2018-03 and 2018-05, April to October 2021 (after 109 resigned), and March–April 2024 (after 108 retired) (q299, q300, q320).
- **Those were bad months for everyone.** In them, the other quoters won 0.187 and took 8.13 days on average. In months when 115 sent no quotes, others won 0.272 in 5.13 days (q299).
- **Comparing within the same month halves the gap.** It falls from -0.071 to -0.031, or -0.030 by customer × quarter (q290). With standard errors clustered by customer, that is about 1.8 SE, not 3.7 (q312, q320).
- **2021 reverses.** That year holds a third of 115's quotes. Matched by month, 115 won 0.125 against 0.119 expected (q315). F6's 2021 deficit came from comparing them with peers who quoted in the better months of that year.
- **115 is no longer the outlier.** With timing controlled, full-time estimator 109 sits at -0.038, and 108 and 109 are 0.071 apart, further than 115 is from expectation (q290, q320).

**What survived:**
- **A smaller gap remains outside 2021,** -0.049 at about 2 SE (q305). It leans partly on 2022, when 115 won 2 of 37 (q315).
- **It isn't explained by quote size or complexity.** 115's quotes are smaller than peers' to the same customer, and adding size to the comparison leaves them at -0.062 (q279, q290).
- **The status data look sound.** Every won new quote has a sales order and no other quote does. Validity is 30 days for everyone, and no lost or expired part was ordered within a year (q281, q283, q286).
- **Turnaround still predicts winning within the same month:** +0.078 for quotes sent in 0–2 days, -0.092 for 8–30 days (q317). That is still a correlation; slow quotes may be the harder requests.

**The money:** comparing within the same month, it's 13.2 wins, $158,802, or $20,872 a year (q312). That is quoted value, not margin. Much of it couldn't have been recovered, because 115 was quoting when no estimator was available to do it instead.

**Revised reading:** the useful finding is about the shop, not 115. When an estimator leaves, quoting passes to people who aren't estimators, turnaround slips, and the shop wins less. The lever is estimating capacity and filling vacancies quickly. 115's remaining gap is worth a conversation over a sample of quotes, not a conclusion about how they quote.

**Still unknown:** the records don't show how requests for quotes are assigned, whether open quotes were followed up, or why quotes were lost. Without those, the remaining gap can't be traced to how the quotes were built.

**Verdict on F6: it stands with changes, and it is much weaker than written.** F6's numbers reproduce exactly (27.7 missing wins, $257,449, $33,837 a year, q312), but its explanation doesn't hold up. I saved the challenge as `challenge.json`.

**Why it changes:**
- **115 isn't an estimator.** HR lists them as an engineer (q276). Half of their new quotes (217 of 430) fall in 14 months right after estimators left: 2018-03 and 2018-05, April to October 2021 (after 109 resigned), and March–April 2024 (after 108 retired) (q299, q300, q320).
- **Those were bad months for everyone.** In them, the other quoters won 0.187 and took 8.13 days on average. In months when 115 sent no quotes, others won 0.272 in 5.13 days (q299).
- **Comparing within the same month halves the gap.** It falls from -0.071 to -0.031, or -0.030 by customer × quarter (q290). With standard errors clustered by customer, that is about 1.8 SE, not 3.7 (q312, q320).
- **2021 reverses.** That year holds a third of 115's quotes. Matched by month, 115 won 0.125 against 0.119 expected (q315). F6's 2021 deficit came from comparing them with peers who quoted in the better months of that year.
- **115 is no longer the outlier.** With timing controlled, full-time estimator 109 sits at -0.038, and 108 and 109 are 0.071 apart, further than 115 is from expectation (q290, q320).

**What survived:**
- **A smaller gap remains outside 2021,** -0.049 at about 2 SE (q305). It leans partly on 2022, when 115 won 2 of 37 (q315).
- **It isn't explained by quote size or complexity.** 115's quotes are smaller than peers' to the same customer, and adding size to the comparison leaves them at -0.062 (q279, q290).
- **The status data look sound.** Every won new quote has a sales order and no other quote does. Validity is 30 days for everyone, and no lost or expired part was ordered within a year (q281, q283, q286).
- **Turnaround still predicts winning within the same month:** +0.078 for quotes sent in 0–2 days, -0.092 for 8–30 days (q317). That is still a correlation; slow quotes may be the harder requests.

**The money:** comparing within the same month, it's 13.2 wins, $158,802, or $20,872 a year (q312). That is quoted value, not margin. Much of it couldn't have been recovered, because 115 was quoting when no estimator was available to do it instead.

**Revised reading:** the useful finding is about the shop, not 115. When an estimator leaves, quoting passes to people who aren't estimators, turnaround slips, and the shop wins less. The lever is estimating capacity and filling vacancies quickly. 115's remaining gap is worth a conversation over a sample of quotes, not a conclusion about how they quote.

**Still unknown:** the records don't show how requests for quotes are assigned, whether open quotes were followed up, or why quotes were lost. Without those, the remaining gap can't be traced to how the quotes were built.
